extracted.intended_audience: university preachers; clergy and teachers preparing sermons for university audiences (Catholic)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and principled guidance for composing and delivering sermons addressed to university men, with emphasis on aiming at definite spiritual ends, adapting method to the academic audience, and avoiding rhetorical artifice. Also discusses the broader university-policy context in which theology competes with modern sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preacher's primary objective
rubrics_metrics.description: The preacher’s object is the spiritual good of his hearers; he must have a definite point before him (Finis prædicanti sit ut vitam habeant homines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fix a single, definite aim (a spiritual good) as the target of the sermon; treat all planning, diction, and manner as subordinate instruments to that end. Example references: St. Francis de Sales, St. Charles. Anti-pattern: preaching for display or miscellany of topics without a clear intended benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim at the object, not at earnestness
rubrics_metrics.description: Preachers should not aim directly to be earnest or eloquent; earnestness naturally follows from having a vivid perception of the object to be achieved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate motives and imagery (e.g., contemplation of the Four Last Things) that produce genuine earnestness. Avoid artificial efforts to seem fervent (e.g., contrived gestures or forced passion), which produce only a pretence of earnestness and are counterproductive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentrate resources on one thing
rubrics_metrics.description: Neglect everything besides devotion to the one objective; display and dissipated energy (feats of rhetoric, mock engagements) undermine the preacher’s aim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Condense and direct all effort toward the central point. Anti-pattern: using sermons as a stage for varied rhetorical display rather than focused persuasion; 'display dissipates the energy' and blunts effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness and simplicity over artifice
rubrics_metrics.description: The highest art is to have no art (artificium summum erit, nullum habere artificium); words should be inflamed by interior affection, not by clamor or immoderate gesticulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for spontaneous, grave, emphatic delivery that reflects interior conviction. Quotations: St. Francis de Sales — 'De corde plus quàm de ore proficiscantur.' Anti-patterns: excessive gesticulation, conspicuous elocution, manufactured theatricality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare a distinct categorical proposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Place a distinct categorical proposition before oneself which can be written down and which guides and limits preparation; preach to bring out that one proposition and nothing else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write the proposition and reject any remark, period, or illustration that does not tend to bring it out. This makes the sermon precise and practical. Anti-pattern: vague generalities about 'virtue' or 'Heaven' without a precise, transferable claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach (doceat) and then move (moveat)
rubrics_metrics.description: The preacher’s duty is to instruct the intellect as well as to move the affections; the act of the intellect should precede that of the affections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure sermons contain clear instruction (doctrine, explanation) before appealing emotionally; St. Antoninus and Ignatian method support intellectual preparation preceding affective response. Example: simple explanations (e.g., of the Mass) often attract more listeners than ornate rhetoric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid preaching multiple subjects in one discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing is so fatal to the effect of a sermon as preaching on three or four subjects at once; even serially delivering several distinct subjects in one sitting amounts to multiple sermons without break.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit each sermon to one proposition; if multiple points are necessary, treat them as separate sermons. Anti-pattern: delivering successive distinct topics as if they were a single unified sermon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt method and subject-matter to the university audience
rubrics_metrics.description: General pastoral precepts must be expanded and adapted when preaching 'in the name of a University to University men'; the subject-matter and method vary according to circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor examples, intellectual depth, and approach to an academic audience; draw on learned sources where appropriate and adjust form to suit university habits of mind. Do not rely solely on general saintly maxims without adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal character and earnestness as persuasive authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal ethical traits and genuine earnestness are among the most authoritative persuasives available to the preacher; 'that which is drawn from personal traits of an ethical nature' carries weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate and let personal character (integrity, seriousness) manifest in sermon delivery; this creates sympathy and persuades by example. Anti-pattern: relying on rhetorical devices while lacking evident moral conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not preach for spectacle; prefer power over eloquence
rubrics_metrics.description: The kingdom of God is not in speech but in power; human accomplishments (eloquence, fetches) are subordinate to the spiritual efficacy of preaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize spiritual efficacy (power) and simplicity over rhetorical flamboyance. Avoid building sermons around displays of learning or oratorical virtuosity that do not serve the spiritual end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of the educational-policy context: sciences can displace theology
rubrics_metrics.description: A contemporary school may seek not to attack Theology directly but to rival it by introducing attractive sciences and studies, thereby displacing theology in the imagination and curriculum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the tactic—leave theology alone publicly while monopolizing modern sciences—and respond by ensuring theology is not excluded from university curricula and by contesting monopolization. Caveat: do not denigrate legitimate sciences; instead insist on their proper, non-hostile application. Anti-pattern: allowing sciences to be monopolized and thereby emptied theology by attrition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer constructive rivalry of studies rather than perpetual controversy
rubrics_metrics.description: Opponents often choose positive competition (promote sciences, make them more attractive) instead of negative controversy; overt attacks elicit defensive polemics and can backfire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid perpetual polemic with opponents where possible; strengthen and exhibit the positive worth of theological and allied studies rather than merely attacking other positions. Anti-pattern: perpetuating contentious disputation that only rallies adherents.
